claims.claim: Children with ADHD show large deficits in overall sustained-attention accuracy on continuous performance tests, but the additional decline with time-on-task is only small to moderate, so the problem is lapses throughout a session rather than a cliff after a fixed number of minutes.
claims.source_title: Evaluating vigilance deficits in ADHD: a meta-analysis of CPT performance
claims.key_numbers: 47 between-groups studies; large effect sizes for overall CPT performance; only small-to-moderate effect sizes for performance over time in the handful of studies reporting it; exact d values not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: Session design should assume intermittent lapses from minute one (short questions, re-ask rather than accept a blank, check working every time) instead of treating the first 20 minutes as safe. The 90-minute shape A is not ruled out by this evidence, but it gets no support from it either; the case for shorter blocks rests on C2, C3 and C13.

claims.claim: In a laboratory study, children with ADHD showed a steeper performance decline as time-on-task increased than children without ADHD, and the authors recommend keeping sessions short and offering short breaks to prevent attentional lapses.
claims.source_title: Time-on-task effects in children with and without ADHD: depletion of executive resources or depletion of motivation?
claims.authors_year: 2017 (Dekkers et al. from memory; authors not confirmed in search summary)
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (task length, sample size and effect sizes not visible)
claims.implication: The 30-40 minute teach segment is the longest unbroken stretch in maths shape A. A scheduled break between teach and practise, rather than a break only 'if frustrated', is the minimum change this ADHD-specific evidence supports. The exact minutes are not given by the study.

claims.claim: Students given pre-scheduled breaks (24 minutes work then 6 minutes off, or 12 then 3) reported less fatigue and distraction and more concentration and motivation than students who chose their own break times, with no loss in task completion or invested effort.
claims.source_title: Understanding effort regulation: Comparing 'Pomodoro' breaks and self-regulated breaks
claims.key_numbers: n = 35 self-regulated, n = 25 Pomodoro (24/6), n = 27 systematic-short (12/3); self-regulators took longer sessions and breaks and reported higher fatigue and distractedness and lower concentration and motivation; no group difference in mental effort or task completion. University students, online self-study; randomisation not explicitly confirmed in search summary.
claims.implication: Fixed break points should be written into the maths and Spanish session skills (for example after the starter and after the teach segment) rather than left to the student or to Claude noticing frustration. The study does not show the 24/6 pattern beats 12/3, so either is defensible; tracker_log_session could record whether breaks were taken.

claims.claim: Spreading study of the same material across separate occasions produces better long-term retention than massing it, and the gap that maximises retention grows as the time to the test grows.
claims.source_title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis
claims.key_numbers: 839 assessments of distributed practice in 317 experiments from 184 articles; inter-study interval and retention interval operate jointly; the interval producing maximal retention increased as retention interval increased. Effect sizes not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: Two full 90-minute sessions on the same day (2 Sep 2026) buy less durable learning than the same time on two days, especially with exams 8-9 months away. If a second same-day session happens it should be a different topic or a short retrieval session; the review_queue's 3-week spaced re-test is aligned with this evidence. No ADHD-specific spacing study was found.

claims.claim: A single bout of exercise produces a small but statistically significant improvement in executive function in children and adolescents with ADHD, on low-quality evidence.
claims.source_title: Intervention effect of a single exercise session on executive function in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a three-level meta-analysis
claims.authors_year: 2025 (authors not shown in search summary), BMC Pediatrics
claims.key_numbers: 12 studies; g = 0.17 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.29), P = 0.007; evidence rated low quality; searches to 6 March 2025.
claims.implication: A 10-20 minute brisk walk or similar before the teach segment is cheap and evidence-consistent as a session opener. The best-known single trial in the pool, Pontifex et al. 2013 (n = 40 aged 8-10, half with ADHD), found better arithmetic and reading after a 20-minute treadmill walk than after seated reading: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3556380. The pooled effect is small, so present it as a helpful routine, not a treatment.

claims.claim: Regular exercise programmes in children with ADHD produce large improvements in inattention symptoms and medium improvements in hyperactivity compared with control conditions, across randomised trials.
claims.source_title: The effects of physical exercise in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized control trials
claims.key_numbers: Five databases searched to November 2014; RCTs only; large effect on inattentive symptoms, medium on hyperactive symptoms; SMD values and study count not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: This lands in the parent's weekly plan rather than in the tutor skill: regular aerobic activity on most days is a supported adjunct to study. The tracker does not need to measure it; a free-text weekly note is enough to see whether bad weeks coincide with inactive weeks.

claims.claim: Exercise interventions have a moderate positive effect on executive-function and motor outcomes in children with ADHD, and longer programmes help more than more intense ones.
claims.source_title: The Effects of Physical Exercise on Functional Outcomes in the Treatment of ADHD: A Meta-Analysis
claims.key_numbers: 10 publications; g = 0.627 for functional outcomes (executive functions, motor skills); longer intervention duration associated with larger effects; effect sizes not related to intensity, mean age or gender.
claims.implication: Consistency over intensity: a modest routine sustained across the months to the exams is the pattern the evidence supports; nothing here favours hard sessions, and the parent should not feel that only vigorous exercise counts.

claims.claim: Physical activity improves overall executive function, especially inhibitory control and working memory, in children and adolescents with ADHD, with moderate-intensity ongoing programmes doing best.
claims.source_title: The impact of exercise interventions concerning executive functions of children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims.key_numbers: 15 studies, 493 participants; large improvement in overall executive function after adjusting for publication bias; inhibitory control large (11 studies, n = 406); working memory significantly improved; intensity and acute-versus-chronic were significant moderators; exact pooled g not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: Inhibitory control is the sub-skill behind the logged 'answer-targeting' and 'submits without working' patterns, and regular moderate exercise is one of the few non-tutoring levers on it. Do not quote a numeric effect to the parent from this source because the value was not visible.

claims.claim: A mechanistic review concludes that acute aerobic exercise can benefit executive functions including sustained attention in children with ADHD, that long-term programmes are consistently positive, and that effects on dopamine and noradrenaline systems are the likely route.
claims.source_title: Effects of Exercise on Cognitive Performance in Children and Adolescents with ADHD: Potential Mechanisms and Evidence-based Recommendations
claims.authors_year: Christiansen, Beck, Bilenberg, Wienecke, Astrup & Lundbye-Jensen, 2019
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary (the review's specific dose and timing recommendations were not visible)
claims.implication: Supports placing the short aerobic bout immediately before the hardest cognitive work (the teach segment) rather than at the end of a session. Because its dose recommendations were not visible, the system should not quote a minutes-per-day figure from this review.

claims.claim: Adolescents with ADHD are much more likely than peers to have disturbed sleep and an evening (late) chronotype, with one clinical sample reporting 63.7% evening types, so a 13-year-old with ADHD is likely to drift later and perform poorly first thing.
claims.source_title: Sleep, chronotype, and behavior in adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
claims.key_numbers: Adolescents with ADHD: significantly higher rates of sleep disturbance and 63.7% evening chronotype versus controls (figure taken from an aggregated search summary; sample size not shown). A separate systematic review reports robust evidence for evening-chronotype predominance in ADHD: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312150025_A_systematic_review_of_circadian_function_chronotype_and_chronotherapy_in_attention_deficit_hyperactivity_disorder
claims.implication: The parent should protect sleep timing (consistent wake time, no late screens on study nights) and not schedule the hardest maths work early. The tracker records neither session start time nor sleep, so nobody can currently see whether weak sessions cluster after short nights; recording session start time in tracker_log_session is the minimum.

claims.claim: Adolescents perform better on fluid-intelligence and executive-function tasks at the time of day matching their chronotype (the synchrony effect), and evening-type adolescents tested in the morning are at a disadvantage.
claims.source_title: Circadian preference and physical and cognitive performance in adolescence: A scoping review
claims.authors_year: 2023 (authors not shown in search summary), Chronobiology International
claims.key_numbers: not shown in search summary; the summary states performance on intelligence and executive-function tests was generally better at optimal times of day, with the effect clearer for fluid than crystallised measures. Supporting adolescent study: Goldstein et al. 2007, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0191886906002947
claims.implication: Home education frees the timetable, so put the maths teach segment (the most fluid, novel work) in late morning or afternoon if she is an evening type, and put retrieval starters or Spanish vocabulary drill in weaker slots. The skill should ask for, or the tracker should record, session start time so exit-ticket scores can be compared by time of day.

claims.claim: Body doubling (working alongside another person, in the room or on a call) is widely used and valued by neurodivergent people, but the evidence is a 2023 survey and small 2025 experiments in adults, not controlled trials in adolescents with ADHD.
claims.source_title: Proposing Body Doubling as a Continuum of Space/Time and Mutuality: An Investigation with Neurodivergent Participants
claims.key_numbers: Survey of 220 people, 198 self-identified neurodivergent, 9 not, 9 unsure; descriptive and qualitative; no efficacy outcome measured. A 2025 EEG study (reported as 26 participants) and VR work exist but are small and in adults: https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3663547.3759743
claims.implication: Having the parent quietly present and working on their own task during practice is a cheap thing to try and note in session summaries, and Claude's turn-by-turn presence may partly serve the same function. Present it to the parent as plausible but weakly evidenced, and do not write it into the skills as a rule.

claims.claim: NICE's ADHD guideline lists 'optimising work or education to have shorter periods of focus with movement breaks (including the use of I need a break cards)', reducing distractions (for example headphones) and reinforcing verbal requests with written instructions as environmental modifications, to be chosen from an assessment of the individual's needs.
claims.source_title: Recommendations | Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management | Guidance | NICE (NG87)
claims.key_numbers: No numeric thresholds; the guideline does not specify how many minutes a 'shorter period of focus' is.
claims.implication: This is the closest thing to official UK guidance on session structure. Write shorter focus periods with movement breaks into both tutor skills, add an explicit no-penalty 'break' command the student can type (the digital equivalent of an 'I need a break' card), and make sure task instructions appear in writing in the chat rather than only being implied.

claims.claim: If she takes ADHD medication, NICE describes the choice of preparation and its timing (for example a modified-release methylphenidate preparation in the morning with an immediate-release preparation at another time of day to extend the duration of effect) as decisions the prescriber makes and titrates to response, so the parent's role is to tell the prescriber when study happens and raise coverage at reviews, not to adjust anything.
claims.source_title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NICE guideline NG87, full PDF)
claims.key_numbers: Search summary: consider a modified-release preparation in the morning and an immediate-release preparation at another time of day to extend duration of effect; immediate-release suitable where flexible dosing is needed; dose titrated to response, usually at weekly intervals. This is cited as guidance only; nothing here is medical advice and medication status is unknown to the system.
claims.implication: Medication should stay out of the tracker's structured data. The only system-level change is indirect: if session start times are logged, the parent can see whether the hardest sessions fall inside the effective window agreed with the clinician, and can take that information to the next review.

caveats: The session's web-search budget was exhausted after 18 searches. Planned but not run: confirmation of the authors of the time-on-task study (C2, attributed to Dekkers et al. 2017 from memory); Cepeda et al. 2008 optimal-gap numbers; Cortese et al. 2009 sleep meta-analysis; Chen & Zhu 2024 single-bout meta-analysis (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/10870547231217321) numbers; NICE NG87 sleep-related recommendations; the ADHD-symptom time-of-day study (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9150742/); and the 2020 acute-activity experiment in ADHD (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7312258/).

No study was found that directly compares study-block lengths (for example 25 versus 45 versus 90 minutes) in adolescents with ADHD. The block-length recommendation therefore rests on NICE's unquantified 'shorter periods of focus with movement breaks' (C13), the recommendation in one ADHD lab study (C2), and a general-population Pomodoro experiment in university students (C3). The evidence is silent on the exact minutes; anything between roughly 20 and 40 minutes of focused work followed by a short movement break is consistent with it, and 90 minutes unbroken is not.

The ADHD-specific time-on-task effect is only small to moderate (C1), so the case for short blocks is driven more by moment-to-moment lapses, general fatigue evidence and mood/motivation benefits than by a dramatic ADHD-specific decline.

Acute-exercise evidence in ADHD is small in size (g = 0.17) and rated low quality (C5). The chronic-exercise meta-analyses (C6-C8) pool small numbers of heterogeneous trials, and Liang 2021 adjusted for publication bias; effect sizes vary considerably across reviews. Newer network meta-analyses exist (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2023.1139263/full and https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2023.1133727/full) but their numbers were not visible in search summaries. A protocol for active breaks in 10-12-year-olds with and without ADHD (Break4Brain, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11583342/) is registered but had no results in the search results.

Body doubling: a general-audience source in the results states the evidence is anecdotal with no controlled research testing effectiveness; a blog-style summary reported 27-30% faster task completion in a 2025 VR experiment, but no primary source URL for that figure appeared, so it is not used in the claims.

Sleep and chronotype figures came from an aggregated search summary: the 63.7% evening chronotype, a '62 studies, 4,462 patients' systematic review count, and a '73-78% delayed sleep/wake cycle' figure (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12728042/) could not each be tied with certainty to the exact source that states them. Direction of the finding is consistent across sources; the precise numbers should be re-checked before quoting.

Time-of-day evidence (C11) is general-population adolescent research, not ADHD-specific, and applies most clearly to fluid tasks. Preckel et al. 2011 (general population) found eveningness correlated negatively with academic achievement (r = -0.14, N = 700) and morningness positively (r = 0.16, N = 3220), probably reflecting schedule mismatch rather than ability: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S104160801100080X

Doing two long sessions in one day: no direct study was found. The recommendation against it is an inference from the spacing literature (C4) and from time-on-task decline (C1, C2), not from an ADHD trial.
Medication (C14) is cited as guidance only. Whether the student takes medication is unknown, and nothing here should be read as advice on dosing or timing; those are for the prescriber.
